about: The words of the chain black_stones (Data/encounters/chain_black_stones_793.json; Design/content/chains/black_stones.md): the quarrel of King Charles and King Offa, the shut ports, and the letter of 796 about black stones and the length of cloaks. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Thiadbod, the reeve Wighelm, Abbot Gervold and the monk Sigewine are the spine's cast; Folkmar the quern cutter, Hildulf (Thiadbod's man at Hamwic), Hunberht the English shipmaster and Gerwin the stone dealer are ordinary invented people. Quoted: in end_peace.reeve_letter, end_peace.reeve_gifts and end_runner.factor_letter the phrases 'go peaceably without any molestation', 'not seeking the cause of religion, but that of gain', 'pay the customary tolls in proper places' and 'a belt, an Hungarian sword, and two silk cloaks' are from Charles's letter to Offa of 796 as given by William of Malmesbury, tr. J. A. Giles, 1847. Everything else from that letter and from the Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12 is our own plain rendering. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Stones nobody fetches

Behind the dams a quern cutter sits on a pile of finished black stones, cut for the English trade and unsold since the ports were shut. Two skippers stand by him, arguing about whose king a Frisian has.
Forty pairs, dressed and pecked. Cut for the English, who grind finer than we do. They have sat here since the kings stopped speaking. Stone keeps. I do not.
The English used to send word what size they wanted. Now nobody sends word of anything. Six pennies the pair, and I am ashamed to say it.
You have stones aboard already. Then you know what they fetch on this river now. Over the sea is another matter, if anyone lets you land.
The king's order was against the English coming here. The English king's is against Franks going there. Whether a Frisian is a Frank depends on who is asking, and what he is given.
They say it began over a wedding. Kings quarrel about daughters and we cannot sell a millstone. I have stopped looking for the sense in it.
Take four pairs on trust and try the Strand
Buy four pairs at his price, six pennies the pair
Leave the stones and ask what the kings fell out over
Folkmar rolls four pairs down to your boat himself and takes no silver. He says to pay him when the English do. She sits a hand lower in the water.
Twenty-four pennies for four pairs, half what they were worth three years ago. Folkmar says that at Lundenwic no one has seen a new stone since the ban, and that they will pay for the sight.

Nobody at Dorestad knows more than this: about four years ago the Frankish king shut his shores to English merchants, the English king shut his to Franks, and the man to ask is whoever stands on the beach at Lundenwic.
Whose man are you
The king's wic-reeve walks down the Strand with two armed men before your keel has touched. No ship of the Frankish king's people is to land here.
Stay in your boat. Where are you out of, and whose man are you?
Dorestad. Then your king is the Frankish king, and my king's beach is shut to his people. I ask once more, in case the answer has changed: whose man are you?
Black stones. I have not seen a new pair on this beach since the year the order came. My own wife grinds on a stone worn as thin as a dish.
And nothing in her worth the trouble of turning you away. That is almost a pity.
This year my king had the East Angles' king's head struck off. I say so that you know what kind of year it is to ask a reeve for an exception.
Give him a gift and a story: Frisians beached here before either king was born
Lie off the beach three tides and let him see who comes to your boat
Put about and go round by Hamwic, where another king's reeve asks less
The reeve hears the story out, weighs the silver in his hand without looking at it, and says that a Frisian is plainly not a Frank, for a month. You may land. He asks your name twice.
For three tides you lie at anchor and nobody comes but women in small boats, asking the price of stones. On the fourth tide the reeve waves you in. He has counted them too.
You put the helm over. The reeve watches you down the river without a word. A man on the next boat says the West Saxon wic is only half shut, and that Thiadbod of Dorestad keeps a man there.
The size of the gap
At Hamwic a man of Thiadbod's is roping bundles for a party of pilgrims. The bundles are square, and heavy for men who own nothing.
The king here is married to Offa's daughter. So the ban is his wife's father's quarrel and not quite his own. That is the size of the gap, and we live in it.
We go to the thresholds of the Apostles. We have no silver, only our prayers and what is on our backs.
What is on their backs is six English cloaks to a bundle. A pilgrim pays no toll. At the Canche a man of ours takes the bundles and the pilgrims walk on lighter, and holier.
I tell you now, before you say yes: if the toll man there opens one, the cloth is his, and there is a fine, and he remembers the boat.
I hear the reeve at Lundenwic offered you a letter and you would not have it. Good. Letters make peace, and peace closes gaps.
Carry six bundles over to the Canche for a third share
Sell your own goods openly here and leave his bundles alone
Buy the pilgrim ale and let him talk

Six pilgrims and six bundles go over with you. At the Canche the toll man blesses himself as they pass. Your third comes to a hundred and ten pennies, and Hildulf says there is more where that came from.

At the Canche the toll man puts a knife through the rope of the first bundle and six cloaks fall out on the mud. The cloth is the king's. The fine is thirty pennies, and he looks a long time at your boat.
You sell in the open market by the hythe, under the reeve's eye, and pay what is asked. Hildulf shrugs. A woman buys a pair of stones and says she had not thought to see new ones before she died.
He is a weaver's son from up the Itchen and has never been further than this beach. By the third cup he has told you the price of a cloak, who ropes the bundles, and a good deal of English besides.
A hazel rod
The reeve comes to your boat alone, after dark, with a sealed letter and a peeled hazel rod as long as a man's forearm and hand.
You went round by Hamwic. I know. I know most of what goes round by Hamwic. I have come anyway, because your boat is small and nobody watches it.
I want a quiet ship. Not Thiadbod's: everyone looks at Thiadbod's. This letter goes over the sea to the Canche, and no one is to know it went.
There is an abbot there who takes the Frankish king's tolls and is my king's friend. Both things are true at once. Put it in his clerk's hand and no other.
And this. My king wants black stones, and this hazel is the length he wants them. Do not lose it, and do not shorten it to fit your chest.
You have carried bundles for Thiadbod's man. I do not ask. I only say that a letter is lighter than cloth and is paid for longer.
Take the letter and the rod to Quentovic
Take them, and name a price for the risk
Say you carry stones, not kings' letters, and go Thiadbod's way round

The letter goes inside your shirt and the rod under the bottom boards. Before you stow it you cut its length into your own gunwale with a knife: two notches. The reeve leaves twelve pennies for the passage.
Forty pennies. The reeve counts them out slowly and says that he had taken you for a different kind of man, and that it is no matter. You notch the rod's length on your gunwale before you stow it.
The reeve puts the letter back in his sleeve. He says he will find another boat, and that he asked you first. At Hamwic, Thiadbod's man will have bundles waiting.
Whose cloth is that
A long boat with twelve oars comes out from under the land and lies across your course. She has more oars than you have men, and the letter is inside your shirt.
Lower your sail. Whose cloth is that, and whose shore did you leave?
The king's word is that no one from Britain and the English people is to touch the shore of Gaul to trade. I did not make it. I row up and down it.
A Frisian. Every boat I stop is a Frisian, and every one of them has just come from somewhere innocent.
Heave to and show the seal: a letter for the abbot who keeps the king's tolls
Heave to, let him search, and say nothing of the letter
Run for the shoal water where twelve oars cannot follow
He turns the seal to the light, does not break it, and hands it back. The abbot is his own lord. He says he never saw you, and that you should say the same of him.
He does not know the seal and cannot read. He keeps you alongside until a clerk can be rowed out from the shore, which takes until the next day. The clerk looks once and lets you go.
They lift the bottom boards, prod the ballast and find a hazel stick, which interests nobody. Nobody searches a skipper's shirt. It costs you the tide.
You put her over the bank with a hand's depth to spare. Twelve oars draw more water than you do. They stop where the sea turns brown and shout a name after you that is not yours.

She touches on the bank and they are aboard before she lifts. They take the cargo for the king and the letter out of your shirt. The officer says the abbot will have it by morning, with an account of how it came.
The abbot's toll house
At the toll house on the Canche the abbot's clerk holds out his hand. On the mud below lies an English ship with a seal on her hatch and a smell of wet wool.
From the reeve on the Strand. I know the hand. Give it here, and tell me who else has held it since he did.
Your letter came before you, in a king's boat, with a tale about a Frisian who ran. My lord has read both. He found the letter the more useful.
So that is the length a king wants a stone. I had thought a king would ask for something longer.
Forty sacks, shorn at midsummer and sealed in her since Lammas. Put your nose to the hatch. I came over thinking the order was forgotten. It was not.
My lord is roofing two churches. The lead for them lies in the English king's hills and may not lawfully come. He prays about it. He also asks every boat.
Give letter and rod into the clerk's hand, as they were given you
Give them over, and ask the English ship's release instead of thanks
First let Thiadbod's man lift the seal with a hot knife, for silver

The clerk runs his thumb round the seal and is satisfied. Twenty pennies, half the toll for a month, and word that the abbot will answer from his own house on the Seine in three weeks: be at Rotomagus.
The clerk goes in and comes out again. The seal is cut from the English ship's hatch that evening. Her master, Hunberht, says nothing for some time, and then asks your name and your port.
The clerk says the ship is the king's matter and not his lord's to give. The English master heard you ask. He nods to you across the mud. Be at Rotomagus in three weeks for the answer.

Behind the salt sheds Thiadbod's man lifts the wax, reads, and sets it back with a warm blade. Ninety pennies. The clerk runs his thumb round the seal and is satisfied. Be at Rotomagus in three weeks.
Ninety pennies behind the salt sheds. The clerk runs his thumb round the seal, stops, and runs it round again. He says nothing at all. He writes something on his tablet that is not about tolls.
What it was about
A boat from Saint-Wandrille lies at the quay of Rotomagus. The abbot has come up the river himself with an answer, and with him an English monk who has seen the inside of the abbey's letter chest.
Forgive me. You are the one with the boat? The English king's letters to the abbot lie in a chest at the abbey, a whole bundle, tied. I was let read the outsides.
It was a marriage. The young Charles was to have Offa's daughter. Offa said: then my son has Bertha. The king was somewhat moved, and shut the sea. Now you know as much as bishops do.
I am copying a book for York in a room with no fire. I have written in the margin that the cold is great. It is the truest line on the page.
My clerk has a careful thumb. I will say this once, and name no one: the next seal arrives as it left, by the merits of Saint Wandrille and for forty good reasons.
Here is my answer for the reeve. It says what my king will bear to hear said, which is more than it did a year ago.
And this cord. It is knotted at the length a cloak was when I was a young man. Their weavers send them shorter every year at the same price. Let them lay it on the loom.
Take the answer and the knotted cord back to Lundenwic
Take them, and stay a week for the monk to teach you what a seal says
Take them, and ask a cask of the abbey's wine for the freight
A letter inside your shirt again, and a cord round your waist under it. The abbot gives twenty-five pennies and his blessing in the same movement. The reeve will look for you within the month.
Seven evenings with Sigewine and a wax tablet. You can now tell an abbot's name from a king's on a seal, and he has given you a riddle about a pair of scales to keep you honest. Then down the river.
The abbot does not say no. He never says no at once. A cask is rolled aboard, and he remarks that the saint's wine is usually given and not asked for.
The length of a king's stone
On the Rhine bank at Colonia a stone dealer has heard that a Frisian boat carried a rod over the sea. He would like to see your gunwale, where you notched it.
Roughouts from the pits in the hills, as they have come down this river since the Romans. I do not finish them. I sell them to men who know what the buyer's hand wants.
They say the English king has asked for a length. The man who knew it would have his stones cut and stacked while the rest of us were still hearing that the ports had opened.
Some here say it is not millstones he wants at all, but black stone for a church. I sell both. I would still like the length.
Sell him the length, notch for notch
Keep the length yours: pay him to cut twelve pairs to it and hold them for you
Show him nothing, and ask what the pits send down this year

He lays a stick along your gunwale and cuts it at the two notches. A hundred and fifty pennies, counted twice. By next spring every dealer on this bank will have the length, and he will have had it first.
Sixty pennies down. Gerwin will have twelve pairs cut to your notches and stacked under straw with your mark on them. He throws in a riddle about a whetstone, because a stone man should have one.

He takes it well enough. The pits send down as many as ever, he says, and with no English to buy them the finished stones lie about at Dorestad for whoever will take them: cheaper there now than here.
A knotted cord
You are back on the Strand with the abbot's answer and the cord. Thiadbod's big ship lies on the beach where no Frankish hull should be, and he reaches you before the reeve does.
While this beach is shut, one Frisian ship lands on it, and it is mine. An answer that went astray would be worth a pound of silver to me. I do not ask you for anything. I only say what it is worth.
My man read the first letter on the Canche, so I know what the second one answers. You have sold me half already. The other half is the dearer.
Why do the Franks want them longer? Wool costs what it costs. A longer cloak at the old price is a gift to a stranger. Will the Frankish king send me the wool?
If you have something for me, I will lay it before the king at the right hour. There are wrong hours. I have learned to tell them apart.
The abbot wants lead. There are eight pigs in the king's store that nobody has counted since the ban. If they left as ballast, I would not have seen them go. I am telling you what I would not see.
Give the reeve the answer and the cord
Give them over, and take the eight uncounted pigs of lead as ballast for the abbot
Let the answer go astray into Thiadbod's hand

The reeve takes the letter and winds the cord round his hand. Thirty pennies. He says that kings answer slowly, and that you will hear it on this beach when there is something to hear. Thiadbod has gone back to his ship.
The reeve takes the letter and the cord. That night eight pigs of lead come down the beach on a hurdle and go under your bottom boards. Nobody counts them out either. She rides stiff and low.

Thiadbod weighs out two hundred and forty pennies in a net shed. You tell the reeve the abbot gave you nothing to carry. He asks you twice. The answer does not change. The cord you drop in the river off the Isle of Sheppey.
Rain on an altar
The toll man of Quentovic looks into your boat, sees what lies under the bottom boards, and sends a boy running for the abbot.
Lead. From where? No. I did not ask that. I was told this morning not to ask that.
My clerk had word of eight pigs of lead. I see bottom boards and bilge water. Tell me the rest yourself. I would rather hear it from you than from a toll man.
Saint Peter's and Saint Michael's stand open to the sky. I will not ask any king's leave to keep the rain off an altar.
I have gone to Offa many times for the king. I will go once more, with the reeve's word in my sleeve and a dry roof to show both of them what peace is good for.
Land all eight pigs openly, on the abbot's word
Say the lead is your own cargo and sell it at the smiths' price
Tell him plainly what became of the lead, and stand to hear the answer

Eight pigs go up the bank on the abbey's own cart, in daylight, with the toll man holding the horse. A hundred and sixty pennies and no toll. The abbot says he will cross before the autumn gales and that you should watch the Strand after Easter.

The abbot looks at you, then at the lead, then at the toll man, and says that the toll is a tenth. The smiths pay well. Lead is dear on this shore while the sea is shut. The churches stay open to the rain.
The abbot hears it out. He says that he has been lied to by better men and told the truth by worse, and that the roofs have waited this long. He does not ask you to supper.
The beach is open
A Frankish ship lies on the Strand with her mast down and nobody shouting at her. The abbot of Saint-Wandrille stands beside the reeve, and both of them are waiting for you.
The king my lord is no longer moved. He writes to yours as to a brother. The merchants of each are to have the other's protection, and if they are wronged they may go to the king himself.
It took a wedding that was never held, a hazel rod, a knotted cord and eight pigs of lead. Saint Wandrille did the rest. I would not care to say in what proportion.
You carried the rod, so you land the first stones cut to it. The king has said it. I asked him at the right hour.
I am told there are twelve pairs at Colonia already cut to the length, under straw, with your mark on them. You knew before the kings did. I will not ask how.
And the cloaks will come at the old length. I laid the cord on one myself this morning. It covered the knot. A small thing, but I am an old man and I ride in the rain.
Ask the king's writing: your goods toll-free on the Strand
Ask the abbot instead: a man of yours in his toll house on the Canche
Ask for ground on the Strand, and the first order for the quern cutter of Dorestad
Your twelve pairs lie cut at Colonia: ask the writing, and sell the first stones yourself

Gerwin's twelve pairs come down the Rhine and over the sea under your mark. Eight sell on the first tide at a price nobody argues with; four stay aboard. Fifteen hundred pennies, the king's writing, and the only stones of the right length in England.

A strip of parchment with the king's name and six crosses: your ship and your goods free of toll at Lundenwic. Twelve hundred pennies for stones to come, and both kings' officers know your name. The ports are open a full year sooner than they would have been.

The abbot does not say no. A man of your choosing will sit in the toll house on the Canche and see every cargo that crosses. Fourteen hundred pennies, and an order for more lead, lawful this time. The ports are open a full year sooner than they would have been.

The reeve paces out ground above the tide line and drives four pegs. The first order for stones goes to Folkmar of Dorestad by name. Nine hundred pennies. The ports are open a full year sooner than they would have been, and forty pairs of stones are no longer anyone's shame.
As a brother
The reeve has a letter read aloud on the Strand by a priest who turns it out of the Latin as he goes. It is from the Frankish king to his own, and it speaks of stones.

The Frankish king writes that pilgrims are to go peaceably without any molestation. But any among them not seeking the cause of religion, but that of gain, are to pay the customary tolls in proper places.
And he writes of the black stones. Send a man, he says, to say what kind, and he will have them given and help with the carrying. In return he asks that our cloaks come as long as they used to.
He sent my king a belt, an Hungarian sword, and two silk cloaks. Silk ones, and long, I am told. A king makes his point how he likes.
My king died three days before Lammas. The stones are still wanted. Mills do not mourn. I am still reeve, this week.
The Frankish toll men now open pilgrims' bundles on the Canche. I hear they began with a list of Frisian boats. I did not write it. I was asked to read it.
You asked for my ship on the Canche when you could have asked for silver. I carry wool for half the minsters of Kent. Tell me what you want carried, and where.
You carried the answer: ask to land the first stones, toll-free by the king's writing
You carried the lead too: ask the writing here and a man of yours at the abbot's toll house
Ask only for the reeve's order for stones, paid down, and his pilot to show you the river
Your twelve pairs lie cut at Colonia: ask the writing, and sell the first stones yourself

Gerwin's twelve pairs come down the Rhine and over the sea under your mark. Eight sell on the first tide; four stay aboard. Eleven hundred pennies and the king's writing. The other dealers' stones arrive a month later, a finger too short.

The reeve says the first black stones on the open beach will be a Frisian's, and yours. A strip of parchment with the king's name frees your ship of toll at Lundenwic. Eight hundred pennies paid down, and an order for six pairs at twice the price.

The king's writing here, and by the abbot's word a man of yours in the toll house on the Canche. Fifteen hundred pennies paid down. You have a foot on each shore, and for once both kings are glad of it.
Six hundred pennies down against stones to come. The reeve's own pilot takes you from the Nore to the Strand and back on one tide and names every bank. You will not need him again.
The quarrel outlives the king
Offa is dead and no letter came. At Hamwic Thiadbod has a tally laid out on a cask head, and half of it is in your name.
Offa died three days before Lammas with his quarrel unmended. The abbot's answer never reached him, as you know. The new king has Kent in arms and no hour for letters.
So the beach at Lundenwic stays shut, stones stay dear there and cheap at home, and the gap here stays the size it was. I said a pound. It has been worth more.
The abbot on the Canche has lost two more summers of tolls and knows which boat carried his answer. He names sums and saints in the same breath. You are among the sums.
The quern cutter at Dorestad still asks after four pairs he gave on trust. He has sixty pairs on the pile now. He says stone keeps.
Take your share of the shut years, and a man of your own in the gap at Hamwic
Take it all in silver, with the marks of the Solent creeks, and be seen with neither of them again
Send the abbot word of what his answer said, late, under your own name

Nine hundred pennies, and a man of yours beside Hildulf at the hythe. No letter about black stones is ever written. The ports stay shut for years yet, and you are one of the two Frisians who do not mind. An abbot remembers your boat.
Thirteen hundred pennies, and Hildulf walks you down the shore at low water and names every creek. No letter about black stones is ever written. You do not go back to the Canche if you can help it.

A monk bound for the Canche carries your word, with your name on it. Thiadbod pays you six hundred and says it is the last. The peace is made the year after, with the new king. The old one never read it. The abbot sends back one line: that late is a kind of honest.
A line for us
The kings have made it up. At Hamwic Thiadbod's man reckons the shut years on a tally stick, and a pilgrim has come home from the Canche with nothing on his back.
The Frankish king has written to the English one, and there is a line in it for us. Those not seeking the cause of religion, but that of gain, pay the customary tolls in proper places.
They opened every bundle on the beach. A man from Rome with a bag of relics, they opened him too. I walked home. I have seen the sea now and do not need to see Rome.
Every summer through the gap is on this stick. Your notches are on the left. It was good while kings were angry, and kings are not angry for ever.
The reeve at Lundenwic let some other boat land the first black stones, toll-free, by the king's writing. I hear you were asked first.
They cut one of your bundles on the Canche, that time. Your boat is on the toll man's list there. I would not land at Quentovic in a hurry.
Take your share, and keep a man at Hamwic for honest trade now the gap is closed
Take silver, and what the shut years taught: every creek and bar of the Solent
Pay the tolls you slipped, before the reeve of the wic as witness, and start clean

Eight hundred pennies off the stick, and a man of yours stays at the hythe to buy cloth in the open. The toll men on the other shore have long memories and a list. Your name is spelled wrong on it, but it is there.

A thousand pennies. And you can now bring a boat into any creek between the island and the Itchen at night, on the ebb, without a light. It is an honest skill. It was not honestly come by, and the toll men know it.

You count two hundred pennies of your share onto the reeve's table and name what they are for. He has not seen that done before and calls a second witness to watch. Six hundred left, the creeks in your head, and your name on nobody's list.

At Dorestad they say it again: the Frankish king has shut his shores to English merchants and the English king his to Franks, these four years, over a wedding that was never held. Black stones cut for the English lie unsold behind the dams.
The kings have made peace. The abbot of Saint-Wandrille crossed to King Offa and came back with it. The Strand is open to Frankish hulls, and a Frisian of Dorestad landed the first black stones.

This year King Charles wrote to King Offa as a brother. Pilgrims go free; traders among them pay toll. The merchants of each king have the other's protection. Black stones are wanted at Lundenwic, and long cloaks in Francia.
King Offa died three days before Lammas and no peace was made with the Frankish king. The Strand is still shut to Frankish hulls. Stones are dear at Lundenwic and English cloth is dear on the Rhine.
A Frisian skipper has sent word to the abbot on the Canche of an answer that went astray two summers ago. They say the abbot will cross to the new English king in the spring.

Dorestad, behind the dams, a grey noon: a broad Frisian quern cutter sits on a stack of round black lava stones with a pecking hammer across his knees; behind him two skippers argue, one in a long blue cloak; ships' masts over the roofs.

The Strand at Lundenwic, low water, morning: a small boat nosing the shingle; an English reeve in a green cloak with a gilt disc brooch holds up his rod of office, two spearmen behind him; thatched houses and looms above the beach.

The hythe at Hamwic, afternoon sun: a Frisian factor ropes square bundles onto the backs of four pilgrims with staffs and scrips; one pilgrim stoops under the weight; a beached boat and the Itchen behind.

Night on the Strand, a horn lantern: the reeve alone, leaning over a small boat's gunwale, a sealed letter in one hand and a peeled hazel rod in the other; the skipper cutting a notch in the gunwale with his knife.

The Channel, a brisk grey day, white cliffs low on the horizon: a long twelve-oared boat lies across the bow of a small sailing boat; a Frankish officer stands in her bow with one hand raised; the skipper's hand is at the neck of his shirt.

The Canche at Quentovic, ebb tide, flat light: a timber toll house on the bank, a tonsured clerk with wax tablets holding out his hand; on the mud below an English ship with a wax seal and cord across her hatch, her master sitting on the rail.

The quay at Rotomagus, a cold bright morning: a portly abbot with a silver cross hands down a sealed letter and a knotted cord from an abbey boat; beside him a tall stooping English monk blows on ink-stained fingers; the old Roman wall behind.

The Rhine bank at Colonia, late afternoon: rough black quern blanks stacked like loaves beside a barge; a Frankish dealer lays a stick along the gunwale of a small boat between two knife notches; the Roman walls and river behind.

The Strand, evening, a big Frisian ship beached in the background: a well-fed skipper in a long blue cloak speaks close to the player's ear; a woman at an upright loom holds a short cloak against a knotted cord; the reeve approaches along the shingle.

Quentovic, rain: a toll man lifts the bottom boards of a small boat to show eight dull grey pigs of lead; the abbot stands on the bank under a held cloak, one hand raised toward a roofless church gable behind the houses.

The Strand in spring sun: a Frankish ship beached with her mast lowered and nobody minding; the abbot and the reeve stand side by side, the reeve holding a strip of parchment; the first black stones are rolled up the shingle on poles.

The Strand, a summer morning, a crowd of weavers and boatmen: a priest reads from an unrolled letter while the reeve listens with his rod grounded; at the water's edge a small boat unloads round black stones; one woman kneels to turn a new quern.

A net shed at Hamwic, dusk, one tallow light: Thiadbod in his blue cloak lays out silver on a cask head beside a notched tally; his factor counts; through the door the empty hythe and a single beached ship.

The hythe at Hamwic, a grey morning: the factor splits a tally stick over his knee; a pilgrim with a staff and no bundle sits on an upturned boat; behind them a cut rope and an empty pack frame lie on the shingle.
Ending picture, the early peace: a Frankish and an English ship side by side on the Strand, a hazel rod and a knotted cord crossed on a pair of black quernstones in front.
Ending picture, the peace of 796: an open letter with a hanging seal, a belt, a sword and two folded silk cloaks on a table; through the door a boat unloading black stones.
Ending picture, the answer sold: a knotted cord sinking in grey river water, and far off the Strand with one ship on it.
Ending picture, the runner: a pilgrim's bundle cut open on a beach, six folded cloaks spilling out, a toll man's knife stuck in the shingle beside it.
